title: हारजित कथामा सीमान्तीयता {Marginality in the Harjit narrative}
nepali: प्रस्तुत लेखमा भवानी भिक्षु (वि.सं.१९६६–२०३८) को हारजित कथामा सीमान्तीयता विश्लेषणसम्बद्ध रहेको छ । सीमान्तीयता दोस्रो विश्वयुद्धपछिको विश्वमा मानव समाजसम्बद्ध हरेक विषयलाई हेर्ने नवीन चिन्तन तथा दृष्टिकोणको रूपमा विकसित सांस्कृतिक अध्ययनको एउटा अवधारणा हो । प्रस्तुत लेखको उद्देश्य मूलतः सीमान्तीयताका सैद्धान्तिक आधारहरूको पृष्ठभूमिमा रहेर हारजित कथाको सीमान्तीय पक्षको विश्लेषण गर्नु रहेको छ । सामाजिक यथार्थवादी विषयवस्तुमा रचित हारजित कथाले पश्चिम तराईको ग्रामीण सामाजिक जनजीवनको यथार्थ चित्रणसहित सीमान्त वर्गका समस्यालाई प्रस्तुत गरेको छ । तत्कालीन सामाजिक संरचनाका अवयवहरूले निर्मित पात्रगत, वर्गीय, लिङ्गीय तथा विचारधारात्मक रूपबाट विभेदकारी परम्परा कथामा चित्रण भएको छ । सीमान्तीयताका आधारबाट पात्रहरूको प्रतिनिधित्व तथा पहिचान प्रस्तुत भएको हारजित कथामा मूलतः निम्नवर्ग तथा नारीहरू सबै पक्षबाट उत्पीडित सीमान्तकृत बनाइएका छन् भन्ने अध्ययनको निष्कर्ष रहेको छ । विभेदक सामाजिक संरचनाले प्रभुत्वशाली तथा सीमान्तकृतमा विभाजित चरित्रहरूलाई सीमान्तीय पहिचानसम्बन्धी वर्गीय, लैङ्गिक, तथा विचारधाराको आधारमा हारजित कथाको पाठपरक विश्लेषण गरिएको छ ।
american_english: This article analyses marginality in the Harjit narrative of Bhavanibhiksu (1966–2038). Marginality, following the Second World War, is a new concept and perspective that has developed within cultural studies across all areas of human society in the post-war period. The main purpose of the present article, situated primarily within the theoretical foundations of marginality, is to analyse the marginal aspects of the Harjit narrative. The narrative of the Harjit created in social realism deals with the actual picture of rural social life in the western plains, presenting the problems of marginalised groups, including lower-class and gendered communities. The characters, their representations and identities presented in the narrative constructed through the constituent elements of the social reality of that time reflect the study's conclusion that the marginalised, particularly lower-class and female groups, have been oppressed from all sides. The characterisation and identification of characters in the text-based analysis of the Harjit narrative has been carried out primarily on the basis of class, gender, and ideological grounds.
british_english: This article analyses marginality in the Harjit narrative of Bhavanibhiksu (1966–2038). Following the Second World War, marginality is a novel concept and viewpoint that has evolved as a notion of cultural study across every subject of human society in the post-war era. The primary objective of the present article, set against the theoretical underpinnings of marginality, is to analyse the marginal dimensions of the Harjit narrative. The Harjit narrative, created within social realism, presents the authentic picture of rural social life in the western plains, depicting the difficulties of marginalised groups, encompassing lower-class and gendered communities. The characterisations and identities of the characters portrayed in the narrative via traditions, class divisions, gender and ideology mirror the study's conclusion that the marginalised — predominantly lower-class and female — are oppressed from every direction. The representative and identificatory characterisation of persons in the text-based study of the Harjit narrative has been conducted principally on grounds of class, gender, and ideology.
australian_english: This piece looks at marginality in Bhavanibhiksu's Harjit narrative (1966–2038). After the Second World War, marginality is a fresh concept and perspective that grew up as an idea in cultural studies across all bits of human society in the post-war years. The main aim of the present article, sitting within the theoretical foundations of marginality, is to go through the marginal side of the Harjit narrative. The Harjit story created in social realism gives a true picture of rural social life out west in the plains, laying out the problems of marginalised groups, including lower-class and gendered communities. The characters and how they're shown and identified in the narrative, made from the bits of social reality back then, reflect the study's conclusion that marginalised folks — especially lower-class and women — get pushed around from all sides. The way characters are characterised and identified in the text study of the Harjit narrative is mostly about class, gender, and ideology.
